title: A teacher
hookLine: a teacher, mentor or guide, chosen carefully: the Buddha told the confused Kalamas to judge teachings by their fruit
tomorrow: what did the first Christians keep doing, every single day?

lines: SOMEONE IS ALWAYS SELLING A PATH.
WHICH OF THEM IS TELLING THE TRUTH?
cards: Scroll long enough and someone is selling a path: a coach, a guru, a course that promises to change everything. Each one sure. Each one hinting the others are frauds.
The Kalamas, people of a town called Kesaputta, lived in that feed without the phones. Wandering teachers kept coming through, each praising his own teaching and tearing down everyone else's.
So when the Buddha came, the Kalamas asked him straight: we're in doubt. Which of them is telling the truth?

teach.b: You'd expect him to say: me. He doesn't. It's right to doubt, he tells them.

teach.h: NOT REPORTS, NOT CHARM, NOT EVEN ME.
teach.b: Then a list of things not to go on alone: reports, tradition, scripture, clever reasoning, a speaker's charm, and even the thought that this monk is our teacher. Some readers hear the Buddha himself in that last one.
Instead, he says, look at what a teaching does. When you know for yourselves that something leads to harm and suffering, and that the wise would blame it, let it go.
When it leads to welfare and happiness, and the wise would praise it, take it up. Then he asks them a question back. When greed arises in a person, is it for their good or their harm?
Confusion? Harm. So, in the Kalama Sutta, a teaching is tested by its fruit, not by fame or certainty.
Does following this person shrink greed, hatred and confusion, or feed them?

teach.h: TEST BY FRUIT, WITH THE WISE.
teach.b: And notice: the wise are part of the test. The Kalama Sutta isn't permission to trust only your gut.
A good guide can be checked, by you and by people who've walked the road longer. Choose that way, and you're choosing a guide, not a master.

how: Buddhists point to the Kalama Sutta: test a teaching by its fruit and by what the wise praise or blame. People on many paths choose a mentor slowly and check their teaching with others who know the road.

o: whoever is most well-known or certain about their path
a mentor chosen carefully by the fruit of their teaching
a book of rules that replaces the need for any mentor

s: the Kalama Sutta says to trust only your own reasoning
clever reasoning is on the list not to go on alone; what the wise praise or blame is part of the test.
the Buddha told the Kalamas not to accept a teaching just because "this monk is our teacher"
some readers hear the Buddha himself in that line.
the Buddha told the Kalamas to follow whichever teacher was most well-known
he told them to look at the fruit: does it lead to harm or to welfare?

games.q: a friend's meditation teacher is warm, well-known and sure of himself, but she's grown more anxious and cut off from her family since joining. by the Kalama Sutta, what matters most?
o: the fruit: her anxiety and isolation are growing, so the teaching deserves a hard look.
his fame: a teacher that well known must be giving her what she needs.
his certainty: a teacher who never doubts is the one to trust.
games.why: The Buddha set fame and charm aside: when something leads to harm and suffering, let it go.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one teacher, mentor or guide you follow, or are thinking of following. Ask the Kalamas' question quietly: around this person, do my greed, anger and confusion grow, or shrink?
Then let the question go, and sit.

wordCard.voice: A teacher: a mentor or guide, chosen carefully, by the fruit their teaching bears, the way the Buddha told the Kalamas.

carryVoice: Keep this one: a guide. Tested by fruit, checked by the wise, never just taken on charm. That's day 1657.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.65 (Kalama Sutta: the rival teachers, it is right to doubt, the list of things not to go on alone, greed, hatred and delusion lead to harm, what the wise praise or blame)
